detail.longDescription: The Top 20 Docker Containers Every Private Investor Should Run There comes a point in every self-hosting project when you realise you have accidentally built a small data centre. It usually starts innocently enough. “I’ll just run Nextcloud.” Then perhaps Paperless-ngx. Then a password manager. Then something for RSS feeds. Then a dashboard. Then something to automate the other things. Before long, there are 27 containers running on a mini-PC under the desk, the network resembles something NASA might use to control a satellite and you have absolutely no idea what half of it does. For the private investor, however, Docker provides an unusually powerful way of building a personal investment infrastructure. Applications can be isolated, upgraded and expanded without turning the underlying server into an archaeological excavation of forgotten dependencies. The trick is knowing which containers are genuinely useful. So here is my shortlist of the 20 Docker containers every serious private investor should consider running . 1. Nextcloud – The Investment Office Nextcloud should be the centre of the operation. Think private cloud storage, collaboration, calendars, contacts and document sharing rolled into one. Every investment gets its own structure: Pipeline → Due Diligence → Portfolio → Exit Add legal documents, accounts, board papers, research and financial models. It becomes your private digital filing cabinet. And unlike a filing cabinet, you can search it without developing a bad back. 2. Paperless-ngx – The Paper Destroyer Investors generate paperwork at an astonishing rate. Accounts, contracts, invoices, tax documents, bank statements, insurance policies and correspondence all need storing. Paperless-ngx uses OCR to make documents searchable and provides tagging and classification. Scan a document and forget about it. Six months later, search for a phrase and it magically reappears. It is the sort of technology that makes you wonder why we spent 40 years pretending filing cabinets were a good idea. 3. SuiteCRM – The Relationship Machine Private investing is fundamentally a relationship business. Founders. Advisers. Accountants. Solicitors. Brokers. Banks. Investors. Introducers. SuiteCRM provides a central database for all of them. Every meeting, opportunity and interaction can be recorded. Over time this becomes far more valuable than a simple contact list. Your CRM effectively becomes a map of your investment network. And that is rather more useful than discovering a former CEO’s telephone number scribbled on the back of a receipt. 4. OpenProject – Due Diligence Central An acquisition is essentially a project involving lawyers. Lots of lawyers. OpenProject provides project management, task tracking, milestones and Gantt charts. Create a standard acquisition template covering: NDA Information request Financial due diligence Commercial due diligence Legal Tax Valuation Negotiation Completion Integration OpenProject can be deployed using Docker Compose, and its own documentation recommends the Compose approach for production deployments. The result is a repeatable acquisition process rather than a collection of increasingly desperate emails. 5. FreshRSS – Your Private Financial Newsroom FreshRSS is one of those applications that looks almost too simple. That is precisely why it is useful. Subscribe to RSS feeds from: Companies Regulators Government departments Financial publications Industry bodies Research sites Portfolio companies You then have one private news feed instead of visiting dozens of websites every morning. FreshRSS has an official Docker image and is specifically designed as a self-hosted RSS aggregator. For investors, this is effectively a low-cost intelligence service. And it doesn’t shout at you about celebrity divorces. Unless you subscribe to the wrong feeds. 6. Metabase – The Numbers Interpreter Metabase turns databases into dashboards and business intelligence. It can answer questions such as: Which investments are performing best? Which portfolio companies are missing targets? How much capital is deployed? What is the average deal size? How long do deals spend in due diligence? Which sectors are receiving the most investment? This is where your collection of databases begins turning into actual intelligence. The objective isn’t to make pretty charts. It’s to make better decisions. Although pretty charts are nice. 7. Grafana – The Investment Control Room Grafana is particularly good at time-series data and monitoring. Use it for: Portfolio performance. Share prices. Interest rates. Inflation. FX. Commodity prices. Cash balances. Property income. Server performance. The last one is important. If your investment dashboard is offline because the server has exploded, you probably want to know. Grafana can therefore monitor both your investments and the machine watching your investments. Very meta. 8. PostgreSQL – The Database Behind Everything PostgreSQL isn’t glamorous. Nobody wakes up thinking, “I really must look at PostgreSQL today.” But it is incredibly useful. It can store: Company information. Investment records. Transactions. Financial data. Portfolio valuations. Research metadata. CRM information. Operational statistics. It provides the structured data layer underneath your dashboards and applications. Think of it as the filing cabinet nobody sees. 9. n8n – Your Digital Assistant n8n is where things become interesting. It connects different applications and automates workflows. A new investment opportunity arrives. n8n can create: A CRM record. A Nextcloud folder. An OpenProject project. A task list. A calendar reminder. An email acknowledgement. All automatically. Automation is particularly valuable to a small investment operation because you probably don’t have six administrators sitting around waiting to rename folders. You have yourself. And you’re busy. 10. Vaultwarden – The Key to the Kingdom Self-hosting without proper password management is like buying a bank vault and leaving the combination taped to the door. Vaultwarden is a lightweight, self-hosted password-management server compatible with Bitwarden clients. Store passwords, secure notes and other credentials centrally. Use unique passwords. Enable multi-factor authentication. Keep the vault backed up. Your investment office will accumulate an extraordinary number of credentials. Banking. Cloud services. Registrars. Government services. Portfolio companies. Servers. APIs. You don’t want to remember them all. You want a password manager to remember them. 11. Gitea – Version Control for the Investment Office Gitea is primarily a Git hosting platform. You might reasonably ask what that has to do with investing. Quite a lot, actually. Investment models evolve. Scripts change. Configuration files get modified. Research databases develop. Automations are rewritten. Gitea provides version control. You can therefore keep a proper history of changes instead of creating: Model_Final.xlsx followed by: Model_Final_2.xlsx followed by: Model_Final_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx A surprisingly large percentage of corporate technology appears to operate on exactly this principle. 12. Vikunja – The Investor’s To-Do List Investing creates endless little jobs. Call broker. Review accounts. Chase solicitor. Read board papers. Update valuation. Renew insurance. Arrange meeting. Vikunja provides tasks, projects, deadlines, priorities and recurring activities. It is deliberately straightforward. That matters. You don’t need a project-management system that requires a project-management project to implement. 13. Uptime Kuma – Is Everything Still Working? Eventually you will have enough containers to forget what is supposed to be running. Uptime Kuma keeps watch. It can monitor websites, services and endpoints and alert you when something stops responding. This sounds trivial. Until the day you discover your document system has been offline for three weeks. At that point it becomes considerably less trivial. It is essentially the digital equivalent of occasionally checking that the office hasn’t caught fire. 14. Nginx Proxy Manager – The Front Door As your number of services increases, you don’t want to remember 20 different ports. A reverse proxy gives your applications sensible addresses and handles HTTPS certificates. Nginx Proxy Manager provides a relatively approachable graphical interface for managing this. Instead of: 192.168.1.20:8127 you can have: crm.yourdomain files.yourdomain projects.yourdomain Much more civilised. It also means you don’t need to explain to visitors why your investment office looks like an abandoned internet café. 15. WireGuard – Your Private Tunnel If you’re accessing the investment office remotely, a VPN is essential. WireGuard provides a fast, modern VPN solution. You can securely connect back to your home or office network from a laptop while travelling. That means your sensitive applications don’t need to be exposed unnecessarily to the public internet. For a private investor, this is not merely technical housekeeping. It is basic risk management. 16. Actual Budget – Personal Financial Intelligence Although designed primarily around personal budgeting, Actual Budget can be useful for tracking personal cash flow and expenditure. For an investor, it can provide a useful distinction between: Investment capital Personal expenditure Household cash Available liquidity The important thing is not to confuse personal budgeting with portfolio accounting. They’re different systems. But having both available can produce a much clearer picture of overall financial circumstances. 17. BookStack – The Institutional Memory This might be the most underrated container on the list. BookStack is a self-hosted documentation platform. Use it to document: Investment processes. Due diligence checklists. Operating procedures. Server configuration. Emergency procedures. Investment policies. Deal templates. Lessons learned. Why something was done. The last one is particularly important. Five years from now, you may remember what you did. You probably won’t remember why. BookStack does. 18. Linkwarden – Save Your Research Investors spend an extraordinary amount of time reading things online. Company websites. Industry reports. Regulatory announcements. Research. News. Competitor information. Linkwarden provides a central place to save and organise useful web pages. Create collections for each investment. Save supporting evidence. Add notes. Build a permanent research archive. That means your investment thesis isn’t dependent upon remembering which website you happened to visit on a Tuesday afternoon three years ago. 19. Stirling PDF – The Document Workshop PDFs are unavoidable. Contracts. Accounts. Reports. Presentations. Due diligence packs. Stirling PDF provides a self-hosted toolkit for manipulating PDF documents. Merge. Split. Convert. Compress. Rearrange. Extract. It is one of those applications you may barely notice until the moment somebody sends you 18 separate PDF files and asks you to turn them into one document. At that point, it becomes your best friend. 20. Portainer – The Container Control Panel Finally, we come to the application that helps manage all the others. Portainer provides a graphical interface for Docker. You can view containers, images, volumes, networks and logs. For someone who doesn’t want to live permanently at the command line, it makes Docker considerably more approachable. It is not strictly an investment application. But once you’re running 20 containers, you will appreciate having a control panel. Otherwise you may eventually find yourself typing commands into a terminal at two in the morning asking yourself why you thought this was a good idea. How They Fit Together The real power isn’t any individual container. It is the architecture. A prospective investment enters SuiteCRM . n8n creates the deal. Nextcloud creates the document structure. OpenProject manages due diligence. Paperless-ngx processes incoming documents. FreshRSS collects relevant research. Linkwarden stores important web sources. PostgreSQL stores structured information. Metabase analyses it. Grafana monitors performance. Vikunja manages outstanding jobs. BookStack records institutional knowledge. Vaultwarden protects credentials. WireGuard provides secure remote access. Nginx Proxy Manager handles the front door. Uptime Kuma watches everything. Gitea records technical changes. Stirling PDF handles document surgery. Actual Budget provides personal financial visibility. And Portainer tries to stop the whole thing becoming a technological crime scene. That is a genuine private investment platform. Don’t Install All Twenty on Day One There is, however, one important warning. Don’t install everything simply because you can. Start with five: Nextcloud Paperless-ngx SuiteCRM FreshRSS Vaultwarden Then add OpenProject, n8n and your dashboards. Only install something when you have a problem it solves. Otherwise you’ll spend three weekends configuring software instead of evaluating investments. This is known in the technology industry as self-hosting displacement activity . It is extremely enjoyable. It is also remarkably unproductive. The Real Cost The software itself can be free. The hardware doesn’t have to be expensive. A sensible mini-PC, decent storage, backup hardware and UPS can create the foundation for the entire environment for well under £1,000. The expensive component is your time. And unlike software licences, that isn’t renewable. The objective should therefore be automation. Build the system once. Document it. Back it up. Maintain it. Then let it quietly perform the administrative work while you concentrate on investment decisions. Final Thoughts Docker has effectively changed the economics of self-hosting. A small investor can now run a collection of applications that would once have required a surprisingly substantial IT department. More importantly, these aren’t simply replacements for Microsoft Office or Google Drive. Used properly, they become the infrastructure of an actual investment operation. The private investor gets a CRM. A document system. A research platform. A project-management system. Business intelligence. Automation. Security. Monitoring. Knowledge management. And all of it can sit quietly on a small server under a desk. Of course, there is one danger. Once you have 20 containers running, you’ll start looking at container 21. Then 22. Then you’ll discover a wonderful open-source application designed to manage your collection of open-source applications. At which point the project has officially become a hobby. And the investment office has become a homelab. There are worse things to do with a Saturday. Just remember to back it up first. #containers #data #docker #openSource #privateInvestment #selfHosting
